title: The Spine and Tooth of Santo Guerro

identifying_description: The object represents a cathedral, inside which lies an actual spine. The cathedral is made of firearm components including shell casings and lead shots. For the green and black patina, Al Farrow used the following products from Sculpt Nouveau: Verde smart stainUniversal verde patinaMint green blue patinaVista green for steelBirchwood Presto Black gel (gun blueing product)Scalecoat I S1001 Loco Black Flat (discontinued)
web_text: This sculpture, made from deconstructed guns and ammunition, also incorporates motifs from European cathedrals, a juxtaposition that draws attention to the historical connection between religious intolerance and warfare. This was particularly true during the medieval Crusades, religious wars that the Roman Catholic Church sanctioned to liberate Jerusalem from Islamic rule. Al Farrow believes that all of the world’s major religions have undermined their moral authority by claiming that “God is on their side” when waging war. Farrow’s cathedral is transformed into a memorial reliquary or shrine by the inclusion of a human spine in the nave and a human tooth—both belonging to the fictitious Santo Guerro (Saint War)—over the transept door. The spine, mounted for display, recalls that many European cathedrals were built with funds derived from the viewing of religious relics. Farrow’s bone-filled reliquaries suggest that it is neither religion nor the human soul that is eternal, but rather the instinct to make war.

PREVIOUS VERSION
The Spine and Tooth of Santo Guerro replicates elements from several medieval European cathedrals, and is fabricated from more than two hundred deconstructed guns, as well as thousands of bullets and shot. Farrow's use of guns and ammunition comments on the historical connection between religious intolerance and warfare—particularly during the medieval Crusades, which sanctioned the violent conquest of the Holy Land. Farrow believes that, historically, all of the world's major religions have undermined their moral authority by claiming that “God is on our side” when waging war.
 
Farrow's cathedral is transformed into a reliquary by the inclusion of a human spine in the nave and a human tooth over the transept door—both ostensibly belonging to the fictitious Santo Guerro (“Saint War”). The spine, mounted for display on a platform covered with 15th-century silk, recalls that many European cathedrals were built with funds derived from the viewing of relics. 

Farrow's bone-filled reliquaries evoke the Catholic Church's core doctrines of mortality and immortality, and thus serve as traditional “vanitas” symbols illustrating the futility of most human endeavors—even the great cathedrals—and the inevitability of death. However, they also suggest that it is neither religion nor the human soul that is eternal, but rather the human instinct to make war.
